common_name: Balmy Lilac Beebalm (Compact Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing generously for airflow.

directions: Balmy Lilac arose as a sport of Balmy Purple and shares the same dense, mildew-resistant Balmy series habit, but opens in soft pale-lilac tones rather than deep purple-red. The tight, globe-shaped flower heads stack on short stems well under a foot tall, making it one of the smallest bee balms suited to container culture or the very front of a border. It still draws hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies in numbers disproportionate to its size through a long early-to-midsummer bloom window. Divide the tidy clump every three to four years in spring to keep it vigorous and to propagate additional starts.

common_name: Balmy Rose Beebalm (Compact Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation between plants.

directions: Balmy Rose rounds out the Balmy series with vivid rose-pink flower heads over dark green, minty-basil-scented foliage, on the same dwarf, densely branched frame that keeps the whole series under a foot tall. Its compact size and above-average powdery mildew tolerance make it a practical substitute for full-size bee balm in small gardens and mixed containers where taller Monarda didyma cultivars would sprawl. Hummingbirds and bumblebees visit the shaggy blooms steadily from early into midsummer. Lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to renew vigor.

common_name: Pardon My Lavender Bee Balm (Extremely Compact Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Pardon My Lavender fills out the compact Pardon Me series in a softer register, bearing pale lavender-pink flower clusters that pair gently with the more saturated Pardon My Cerise and Pardon My Purple in a mixed planting. Its dark green foliage carries markedly better powdery mildew resistance than older, taller heirloom bee balm cultivars, so it stays presentable through a full humid summer. The dense, well-branched mound draws bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies especially heavily when planted in drifts. Give it adequate spacing for airflow and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to sustain flowering.

common_name: Leading Lady Orchid Bee Balm (Extra-Compact Early-Blooming Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Leading Lady Orchid is a densely branched, non-running hybrid that begins flowering earlier than most bee balm.

directions: Leading Lady Orchid produces orchid-pink flower heads finely dusted with fuchsia spots on a low, wide-spreading mound that stays well under fifteen inches tall while reaching over two feet across, so give it room to fill in rather than crowding it as an upright cultivar. Like its sibling Leading Lady Plum, it flowers earlier in the season than most Monarda and carries strong resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures older bee balm foliage. Hummingbirds, bumblebees, and butterflies work the blooms heavily from early into midsummer, and the aromatic foliage is largely ignored by deer and rabbits. Deadhead spent heads to tidy the clump and divide every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Leading Lady Lilac Bee Balm (Extra-Compact Early-Blooming Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this 2015 Walters Gardens introduction is a compact, non-running bee balm.

directions: Leading Lady Lilac carries pale lilac-purple flowers freckled with dark purple spots on the same low, densely branched, wide-spreading frame as the rest of the Leading Lady series, forming a tidy non-running mound rather than an expanding colony. It flowers from early to midsummer, weeks ahead of many taller heirloom bee balms, and was bred for markedly better powdery mildew resistance than older Monarda didyma selections. The blooms are a strong draw for hummingbirds and butterflies, while the pungent foliage discourages deer and rabbit browsing. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to keep the planting vigorous and well-aerated.

common_name: Bee-You Bee-Bright Bee Balm (Compact White-Flowered Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bee-Bright is the white-flowered member of the Dutch-bred Bee-You series.

directions: Bee-Bright is the pure-white counterpart to Bee-Happy in the Bee-You series, holding clean white flower heads over a compact, well-branched mound that stays notably free of the powdery mildew that plagues many older bee balm selections in humid summers. Its pale color makes it a useful mixer for softening the hot reds and magentas of other Monarda in a border, and it draws bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies just as reliably as its more brightly colored relatives. Site it in full sun with good air movement between plants to keep the foliage at its cleanest. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain a tidy, floriferous habit.

common_name: Bee-You Bee-Free Bee Balm (Compact Electric-Purple Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bee-Free is a compact, highly mildew-resistant member of the Bee-You series.

directions: Bee-Free bears shaggy, electric-purple flowers opening from magenta buds over deep purple centers, a saturated color that reads vividly even from a distance and makes it one of the more eye-catching entries in the Bee-You series. The compact, bushy habit and exceptional resistance to powdery mildew let it hold clean foliage through a full humid summer where older purple bee balms typically decline. Bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies visit the blooms heavily from early to midsummer. Provide good air circulation and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to sustain vigor.

common_name: Bee-You Bee-Merry Bee Balm (Compact Coral-Pink Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bee-Merry is a low, dense member of the Bee-You series bred for strong mildew resistance.

directions: Bee-Merry opens vibrant rosy-coral flowers from magenta buds on one of the shortest plants in the Bee-You series, staying under fifteen inches tall in a dense, floriferous mound. The warm coral tone stands apart from the more common purples and reds of other bee balm cultivars, giving it a distinct role in mixed pollinator plantings. It shares the series' strong resistance to powdery mildew and keeps attracting hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies through a long summer bloom season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain a tight, vigorous habit.
